## Welcome to SPPH 604 {.center}

**Application of Advanced Epidemiological Methods**

- An **applied, data-intensive capstone**: epidemiological reasoning through real analysis
- The goal is to move from theory to **reproducible, defensible practice**
- We use **just-in-time learning**: methods arrive when your analysis needs them
- **Today is a one-off orientation:** Thursday, Sept 10 · 10:00–12:00 · Zoom

## The big idea: one paper, all term

You choose **one recent, open-data paper** and work with it throughout the course.

**Replicate → Review → Improve → Defend → Synthesize**

- **Replicate & interrogate** your own paper
- **Review** another group's replication
- **Improve** your own analysis in response to the critique you receive
- **Defend** what you changed — and what you chose not to change
- **Synthesize** the final argument in a short reanalysis letter

::: {.notes}
This is the core course map. Explicitly distinguish REVIEW from IMPROVE: M2 is about another group's M1; improvement to your own project happens after you receive review and is defended at M3. (~6 min)
:::

## What each milestone asks you to do

- **M0 — Feasibility:** prove that your chosen paper can support the whole course
- **M1 — Replicate + interrogate:** rebuild the main result and identify the **dominant threat**
- **M2 — Review:** test and critique **another group's M1** professionally and constructively
- **Between M2 and M3 — Improve:** decide which reviewer points to act on in **your own** analysis
- **M3 — Defend:** explain what you changed, what you rejected, and **why**
- **M4 — Synthesize:** turn the full argument into a concise reanalysis letter + reproducible archive

::: {.notes}
The key conceptual distinction: students are not obliged to follow reviewer recommendations, but they are obliged to answer them with evidence and reasoning. (~7 min)
:::

## Choosing your project: the M0 feasibility gate

A paper qualifies only if your group can point to all six:

1. **Reconstructable public microdata**
2. A clear **primary exposure/predictor and outcome**
3. Plausible **measured confounders** for a defensible adjustment set
4. Enough **observations/events** for the main analysis and at least one subgroup/interaction analysis
5. The **design variables** your analysis has to respect — survey weights/strata/PSU, or follow-up time and censoring
6. A **genuine incomplete-observation problem** — a variable your locked analysis uses that is missing for records which should have carried it

**Do not add variables simply to manufacture a missing-data problem.**

::: {.notes}
M0 is a feasibility memo with specific pointers: variable names, files, sample sizes, evidence from the actual paper and data. Criterion 5 is not waivable and is not survey-only: complex-survey weights/strata/PSU is the normal route, a time-to-event structure whose handling can be interrogated is the other, and the group names the feature and the variables that encode it. A paper with neither has nothing to do at P4 — and clustering or repeated measures do not count, because we do not teach the methods that handle them. Criterion 6 is missingness on the analysis variables, not cohort shrinkage — designed subsampling, eligibility, the disease definition and linkage failure are what you must tell it apart from and report at P5, not what clears the gate. It must arise from the locked analysis, and the test is not size: ask whether you could have known in advance that handling it would change nothing. (~8 min)
:::

## BREAK — 10 min {.center}

Back in 10; then reproducibility, AI, and collaboration.

## Reproducibility is the standard

- Every submitted **number, figure, and table** should be generated by code
- The pipeline must run **start to finish on a fresh machine** without manual intervention
- Your group works in a **shared private GitHub repository** during the term
- **M1 and M4** include a downloaded reproducible repository **zip**
- **M2 is slides only** — you rerun the assigned group's M1 materials, but submit no new code archive

> Code that only works on one person's laptop is unfinished analysis.

::: {.notes}
Make the submission rule precise: do not say “zip at every milestone.” Repository visibility should remain private during the term unless the instructor approves otherwise. (~7 min)
:::

## AI is a co-pilot — accountability stays with you

- AI tools are **permitted; none is required**
- You may use them for appropriate coding, debugging, drafting, and preparation **within the rules of each assessment**
- You remain responsible for **auditing the code and defending the epidemiological reasoning**
- M0, M1, M2 and M4 each carry a **cover note**: contributions, external feedback, AI use
    - final slide or final page of what you submit — plus `COVER-NOTE.md` in the repo zip at **M1 and M4**
- **M3 preparation is unrestricted and undisclosed** — rehearse with an AI if you want; there is no M3 submission to disclose it in
- **Presentation:** use everything you prepared — slides, your own speaker notes, your own code and output
- **Q&A:** the answer is yours, spoken — no prepared answer read aloud, no help from anyone in any channel, nothing produced during the session (no AI, no live prompting, no messages)
- Supports approved through your **Academic Accommodation Letter** are the exception, arranged in advance

**“The AI made a mistake” is not a defense for an unaudited result.**

::: {.notes}
Frame this as accountability-first rather than as a ban. Students who choose not to use AI are not disadvantaged. Direct them to the per-assessment AI table in the syllabus for details. (~8 min)
:::

## M2 has special confidentiality rules {.scrollable}

When you review another group's unpublished M1:

- **Paste what is yours or public; describe what is theirs**
- Yours or public: your `sessionInfo()`, your install log, package documentation, an error stripped of their code and numbers
- Theirs: every line of their code, slides, output, logs, results — not a snippet, not a screenshot, not retyped
- If you cannot ask without quoting their work, **ask the teaching team**
- AI must **not generate the substantive critique** for you
- Reviewed material is **confidential** and may not be circulated outside the review assignment
- Never copy or adapt their code, text, figures, output or distinctive implementation
- **Credit does not make it permitted** — their solutions stay theirs
- A general insight may send you back to *your own* analysis: redo it yourself, disclose it
- Your review group writes the review **together**; you do not coordinate with other groups
- Your critique should identify real issues — or explain, with evidence, why the work is sound

::: {.notes}
The old wording banned uploading their work and permitted "debugging help" in the same breath, and students could not tell where the line was. The line is the input, not the topic: their content never goes in; your machine and public documentation always can. On appropriation the rule is short: nothing of theirs is copied or adapted into your own work, credited or not, and a general insight only sends you back to your own analysis — which you then justify, implement and disclose yourself. Say plainly that reviewers award no marks — the teaching team grades the critique — so there is no score to trade, and "coordinate" never meant their own review group. (~6 min)
:::

## Our demonstration paper *(the only paper slide today)*

- **Kueh et al., BMJ Open 2026 — MASLD & NHANES 2007–2018**
- Adults with fatty-liver disease classified into **four body-shape groups** using BMI × waist-to-height ratio
- **Headline:** the non-obese/high-waist group shows the poorest survival
- Across the term, we will **rebuild the analysis from public data and interrogate the choices behind it**

> Today is the *what* and *why*. The methodological *how* begins next week and unfolds just in time.

::: {.notes}
Keep this as a hook only. Do not teach FLI, the phenotype definitions, survey weights, or missing-data details today; those are introduced in the weeks that need them. (~5 min)
:::
